title: Rubio Says Trump Is Coming to India. The Trade Deal, He Says, Is 'on the Last Inches.'
excerpt: In separate White House interviews, America's top diplomat and its envoy to India described the relationship as 'stronger than ever' — and signalled a presidential visit early next year.
body:
The last time a sitting American president visited India, it was February 2020. Donald Trump landed in Ahmedabad for the 'Namaste Trump' rally — a spectacle of 100,000 people, a new cricket stadium, and a lot of diplomatic fanfare. Five years and a pandemic later, he may be headed back.

In separate exclusive interviews with the Indian news agency IANS at the White House on Saturday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor laid out what amounts to the clearest public roadmap yet for the next phase of India-US ties: a presidential visit early next year, a trade deal in its final stages, and a partnership both men described as "stronger than ever."

## 'We're on the Last Inches'

Rubio was direct about the trade deal. "We're hoping to finalise a trade deal. We're on the last inches of getting it done, and it's very positive," he told IANS.

Gor, who had been in meetings with US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and India's Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal in New Delhi just 48 hours earlier, offered more texture. "There's a handful of issues that remain. A lot of it now is on the language that ultimately both sides will sign."

The deal, in its broad strokes, has been taking shape since February 2025 — when both countries agreed to an 18 per cent tariff on Indian goods in exchange for India lowering trade barriers and importing more American products. But it was derailed when the US Supreme Court invalidated Trump's sweeping global tariffs, and further complicated by a USTR Section 301 probe into alleged overcapacity and forced labour.



> **""We have so much aligned and in common — on economics, on supply chains, on critical minerals, on energy, on security, on freedom of navigation."**


Both Rubio and Gor expressed confidence the remaining issues would be resolved in "weeks or months." Gor compared the pace favourably to the India-EU trade talks, which have been running for nearly two decades without a deal.

## H-1B Review Is Not Targeting India, Gor Insists

For the roughly 750,000 Indian professionals in the US on H-1B visas — and the hundreds of thousands more waiting in line — Gor had a specific message: the Trump administration's review of the visa programme is not aimed at India.


![White House — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/White_House_north_and_south_sides.jpg/3840px-White_House_north_and_south_sides.jpg)


"The changes are part of a broader overhaul of America's immigration system," Gor told Outlook Business. He added that the focus on curbing illegal immigration aligns with India's own position, and the review should not be read as targeting any particular country.

That reassurance, if it holds, matters enormously. Indian nationals receive the overwhelming majority of H-1B approvals each year, and any systemic changes ripple through the diaspora — from tech workers in Silicon Valley to consulting firms in Chicago.

## A Presidential Visit Takes Shape

On the question of Trump visiting India, Rubio left little ambiguity. "I look forward to returning myself before the end of the year and setting up a presidential visit in the early parts of next year," he said.

India has been pressing for a Trump visit for months, potentially as part of a broader engagement that would include Japan and Australia — the Quad partners. A visit would be a powerful signal of normalisation after a year of friction: Washington imposed high tariffs on Indian goods, punished New Delhi for continuing to buy Russian oil, and leaned closer to Pakistan. The killing of three Indian sailors in US Navy attacks on commercial ships in the Gulf of Oman roiled relations further.

Rubio acknowledged the breadth of the partnership. "We have so much aligned and in common — on economics, on supply chains, on critical minerals, on energy, on security, on freedom of navigation. We're aligned on so many things."

Gor called the bilateral relationship one of "limitless potential" and praised Modi's leadership style: "He is incredibly dynamic, incredibly hands-on, and results-driven. In a way, I see a lot of similarities between him and President Trump."

## What This Means for the Diaspora

A Trump visit to India would likely come as a package — a signed or nearly-signed trade agreement, expanded defence and technology cooperation, and a public reaffirmation of strategic ties. For the 5.1 million-strong Indian-American community, the stakes are tangible: tariff outcomes affect businesses, H-1B policy shapes careers, and the broader diplomatic temperature influences everything from visa processing times to the reception Indian professionals face in American workplaces.

If the trade deal does close in the coming weeks, it will be the first bilateral trade agreement India has signed with the United States — a milestone decades in the making.
